utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to put on the record that the Chamber has accommodated a request by Mr. Harland for a later start today. That is the reason why we're sitting from 10.00 until 2.45, so that we are able to finish Mr. Harland's testimony today. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harland. Please be seated. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Lukic, you've got until a quarter to 2.00 this afternoon. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Can you turn on your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Great. And will I need the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the hard copy could be provided to Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court document 8163.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for it to come up, Mr. Harland, let me just tell you that this is your document dated the 10th of December, 1994, since that is where we were left -- where we left off?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... I hear nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe channel 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This will be the English interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can you speak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is one of your documents dated 10th December 1994, and if we could just see page 3 of this document, paragraph 3, from the top. This is where we left off on Thursday, and you said - we see that at the bottom of paragraph 3: [In English] "US and French officials have noted that UNPROFOR's departure would give the international greater 'flexibility' in dealing with the Serbs." [Interpretation] Did that mean that NATO would be freer to target Serbian positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not so much NATO and the United Nations as certain nationalities, but certainly the United States and also certain individuals were much more in favour of the use of force and felt that the departure of UNPROFOR could facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 156 of your statement - and that is the relevant paragraph - you say: "He openly said," referring to Milan Gvero, "that Serbs would not respect the safe areas until they're demilitarised." According to you, is this position of his appropriate or is it wrong? What did you consider, you at UNPROFOR, what the Serb position should be? What was your official position on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was deeply divided. My counsel was that the principal mandate was to deter attacks against the safe areas by all means necessary, so demilitarisation should not be a requirement unless - as in the case of Srebrenica and Zepa - there happened to be a bilateral agreement to that effect; but it was a major debate throughout the history of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to paragraph 160. We're in January 1995 now and you say: "On 11 January 1995, Mladic, Delic, and Blaskic," these were three generals of the three Bosnian armies; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They signed the agreement on the military implementation of the cessation of hostilities agreement. And then in document - could we please have it up on the screen -- actually, it's the same document but we need page 7. [In English] "Muslim-Croat relations took a few more small steps forward this week. As before this seems not so much significant commitment to the Federation as it does to accepting the present division of territory and populations." [Interpretation] These notes of yours, do they actually confirm that everyone in Bosnia and Herzegovina was in favour of partitioning the territory and the ethnicities to move to the relevant -- to the respective territories under the control of their own forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, in general, the position of the leaderships of the three communities and had considerable support within the three communities, though there were substantial minorities, mainly the urban middle class, who still seemed to aspire even at this late stage in the war to some sort of collective life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have difficulties in finding your quote on page 7 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, "Federation issues," on top of the page, Your Honour. The very first paragraph on the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is page 6 in e-court, Mr. Lukic, 6 out of 7 in e-court. I found it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just to be clear, it's page 7 of the document. I don't know how is it loaded in e-court. It's page 7 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 167 of your statement, where you say: "The Bosnians are reorganising, replenishing, and retraining and very soon they will have an overwhelming force and it will become an important factor in terms of personnel." Can you tell us how Bosnians managed to arm themselves in spite of the embargo? What channels did they use?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was several and they changed over time. We were aware that Iran was providing weapons through Croatia, with the knowledge of the United States and others, and that those weapons were permitted to transit through Croatian territories subject to a sort of tax. A certain amount of those weapons would have to be passed on to Croat forces. About this time, too, I believe that there were low-level air-drops into Tuzla airport by supporters of the Bosnian government in the west and in Turkey. So there were multiple channels. There were also some weapons purchased locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What measures did UNPROFOR take in order to implement the embargo and could it have done anything in that respect? Was it in that position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was in UNPROFOR's mandate to prevent the purchase or the supply of weapons. When there was a demilitarisation agreement in place, there would often be an inspection regime agreed by the parties for UNPROFOR and then there would be a role, like in theory in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it then who was supposed to implement -- to enforce the embargo in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The Security Council, I think, had a sanctions regime and it had a mechanism it had put in place outside of UNPROFOR to impose sanctions of countries that violated. But in fact, of course, the mechanism was never used, given that some members of the Security Council were, of course, involved in the supply of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is my next question. The air-space was under NATO control and UNPROFOR, as you say. There were low overflights. And that was one of the ways that the weapons were distributed, including by Turkey, who was a NATO member. Were there any other countries that you're aware of that provided weapons by air?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to what appears to be Mr. Lukic providing information or evidence to the Chamber with respect to the whole first part of that question. He's moved on now to something different, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, if you say whether any other countries, where you have testified more or less that it was Turkey, who -- that I think is not appropriate. Is there any dispute about it, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to familiarise myself with the evidence. I don't know that the Prosecution would dispute in terms of this case, but of course I wouldn't want to agree to a fact unless I could verify its accuracy myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness just mentioned Turkey and low flights dropping armament in Tuzla area, so I was just repeating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, did you mention that Turkey dropped weapons above Tuzla in low flights?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I should clarify that our source was only the Bosnian government 2nd Corps, the Tuzla Corps. We had direct observation from our military observers of the flights, but obviously those who made the flights didn't tell us who they were, though of course they were able to get passed NATO monitoring, so there was that, and we were able to see what type of aircraft they were and that they were dropping equipment. But they did not co-operate with us. We raised the issue with NATO 5 ATAF, the NATO air forces, but they did not co-operate in providing further information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, the transcript on page 5 is not entirely clear, but I can imagine that you've understood it that Turkey was performing low-level air-drops. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 168 you say another meeting was held between the new commander of UNPROFOR, BH UNPROFOR, General Smith and General Mladic on the 7th of March, 1995, in Vlasenica, when Mladic told Smith that Bosnian Serbs intended to attack and significantly suppress the three enclaves in Eastern Bosnia. So this was openly stated and it was no secret?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at that meeting, though other Serb leaders said the same things to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 5726, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This -- these are minutes from a meeting of the General Staff -- of the Main Staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here we can see under item 5, paragraph 5, on top: [In English] "Mladic questioned General Smith on the military situation and the activities of BH within the Srebrenica pocket. General Smith reported that he had not seen any weapons within the town and that he had inspected the WCP." "WCP" is weapons collection centre --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- or points?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] You told us on the first day of your testimony that the international community was open towards the Serbs. Was General Smith truthful where he spoke here and uninformed about the existence of these weapons or was he not telling the truth to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution objects to the witness being asked to comment on the truthfulness or untruthfulness of another witness in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Lukic may ask whether this witness is aware of any knowledge of the person speaking contrary to what he said so -- but that's a factual question then. Have you any knowledge about Mr. Smith having knowledge which did not correspond with what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Smith actually told me the same, that weapons were not visible in the town. I think most of the weapons were deployed -- there were a lot of them, maybe 10- or 12.000 all together deployed -- light arms mainly, deployed on the confrontation lines and -- rather than in the town. And when they were in the town, they didn't show the weapons publicly. So strictly speaking, I believe what General Smith has probably said is probably true, that he did not see them in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not ask for 65 ter 10594 to be pulled up, but this is a document about a meeting, a regular monthly meeting, held on the 25th of March -- 21st of March --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995. And there is an acronym mentioned in the document, CAC. Who was CAC at the time and what does this acronym stand for? Was this Mr. Enrique Aguilar at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it stands for civil affairs co-ordinator. It was my boss, the chief political officer. This Aguilar had just replaced Andreev.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that day he stated that the international community could not come up with a long-term solution to this conflict. Was that the general position within UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was a growing view in UNPROFOR that the international position of trying to secure a cease-fire first and then allow space for negotiations was not working, and there was a view in UNPROFOR that force would have to be applied to the Serbs to create an incentive also for them to negotiate that long-term settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that the Serbs themselves kept offering a permanent, lasting solution to this conflict, and that the Muslim side was the one that did not want a long-lasting solution, but rather just temporary cessation of these conflict -- of this conflict. Isn't this something that we've already established during your examination?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was the problem in a way. The Serbs at that point held about 70 per cent of the territory, and so they wanted to freeze the situation there and that removed the incentive for them to settle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't this a matter which has been dealt with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- extensively. Mr. Lukic, there's no need to repeat evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But that's my next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay then your next question -- then please your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The military pressure on the Serbs, was it supposed to be applied not in order to end the war but rather so that they would cede the territory that they were holding to the other side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a growing view in UNPROFOR that those two were closely connected, that force would be required in order that the Serbs would lose territory and then have a greater incentive to settle for -- along the agreed territorial lines of 51/49.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that any or every agreement on a temporary cessation of -- or cease-fire was used by the Bosniaks to arm additionally?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly there was a progressive rearmament of the Bosniaks and training and equipping over the whole three-year period. I think that's why just about at this moment the Serbs changed from a strategy of assuming that time was on their side to attempting a more rapid military resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have document 10111.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the document to come up - and we need the first page - let me ask you this: Is it correct that the Muslims, and you've already partly confirmed that, were preparing for an offensive in the spring of 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's correct that all three sides were going to try to resolve the conflict militarily during 1995. Yes, we saw those preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the international community did not exert pressure on the Muslims at this time, as well as previously, in order to find a solution to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had varied greatly over time. President Izetbegovic told me that he regretted that he had been encouraged not to sign the Cutileiro Agreement in 1992, which was generous to the Bosniaks. There was pressure, some pressure, on him to sign 1993, which they did not, Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. They did agree to the Contact Group plan in 1994. And by the beginning of 1995, they were subject to pressure to accept the 51/49 formula.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of the document we have before us and paragraph 2, there is mention of two major offensives launched by the Muslims against Serb positions. And it says that the BH Army - that's in paragraph 2 under (a) - in both areas, and it is a reference to Vlasic and Greda feature, used heavy artillery and mortars in preparation for the commitment of a considerable number of infantry, in some cases with the support of tanks. So this is the period when the Muslim forces had in their position heavy weaponry, mortars of high calibre, and other major pieces -- artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, though still not in considerable numbers, and at this point their military activity was still not closely co-ordinated with UNPROFOR and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 171 of your statement you say: "As the Serbs steered towards the military option, conditions in Sarajevo deteriorated." Would you agree with me now that what you said here in your statement is not correct, that the Serbs were not making preparations for military action and that all their actions were actually a response to the Muslim offensives?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's correct. What I said earlier was that we had come to the conclusion that all three sides - Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats - were going to make an attempt to militarily resolve the war on terms favourable to themselves. And this does record an uptake in Serb military activity, even though there was also a parallel Bosnian increase.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the same time when actions by the Muslim army were being carried out against the Serb position, General Soubirou's forces were simultaneously engaged in rapid actions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the interpretation. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this same period, i.e., the end of March 1995, was there an operation launched by UNPROFOR rapid reaction units?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Fair enough. [Interpretation] Also during that same period, the bulk of the weapons in Sarajevo arrived under the Butmir airport, which was under the control of UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- no serious amount -- no heavy weapons arrived into Sarajevo because the only access was through the tunnel which was only about this wide. But it's certainly true that small arms flowed backwards and forwards in large numbers through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "about this wide," can you please tell us for the record how wide it was if you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than 2 metres from the section I went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraph 172 you go back to the issue of sniping. This is April 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court document 10119.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This document shows - and I'm talking about page number 3 in e-court, where there is mention of an anti-sniping project, you mentioned that as well on Thursday, and you made reference to the material that was requested in order to construct barriers that would protect civilians. Here we see on e-court page 4 that for the Bosnian side a total allocation was approximately 3.000 metres of plastic sheet and for the Serbian side, on the next page, we see that the allocation was 3500 metres of the plastic sheet. This demonstrates that the both sides required on the Serbian side an even larger quantity of sheet in order for them both to be protected from the other side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we see document 3507. [In English] Give me one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is related to paragraph 175 of your statement where you say that Karadzic stated the following: "We believe we will have to put an end to the war by military means." However, in -- what you noted in your document of the 22nd of April, 1995, which is on page 2 of this document, fourth paragraph from the top, you noted Karadzic as having said the following: [In English] "'As for the military front, it is clear that the Muslim side remains engaged in unsuccessful offensives. Our counter-offensive is very moderate (in its intensity) and we are trying to give the peace a chance until the end of current cease-fire. However, we believe that we shall be forced to engage ourselves into a drastic counter-offensive, i.e., to put an end to the war by military means. We believe that the international community has to decide what it wants (to achieve) here. If they want war, then they are doing the right thing. All moves of the international community has been very productive in terms of extending the war. If they want peace, then they have to turn a completely new page ...'" [Interpretation] Would you agree with me if I said that the general position of President Karadzic was not war but, rather, peace and that the war should have continued only in the form of a counter-offensive?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the date of this document, but certainly Mr. Krajisnik told me, as did Colonel Indjic and as General Mladic seemed to indicate to General Smith, that in the late winter or early spring of 1995, the Serbs had actually taken a decision to try and bring the war to a military conclusion or at least to accelerate the militarisation, perhaps unaware that the Bosnians and the Croats had done the same thing at about the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you were asked about the position taken by Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then to say that others said something which is in line what you ascribed to Mr. Karadzic is, of course, not an answer to the question. Please, if you want to answer the question, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that by this time Dr. Karadzic was fully committed to intensified military operations and that - as was often the case - he was probably not telling the truth, but rather giving a pretext for accelerated military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is your interpretation of his words, but it does not reflect what he actually said and what you noted down.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, it certainly didn't reflect what he said, but I actually didn't note this down. I see this document was drafted by somebody else quoting his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That was my objection, but the witness has clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] We need page 4 of this same document, third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A minute ago we saw that the Muslims were armed -- arming themselves, that they were reinforcing their manpower, and on this page we can see in paragraph 3 that Dr. Karadzic again is saying the following: [In English] "'The Muslims do not want to extend the Agreement since they believe they are strong enough to defeat the Serbs. However, after their offensives would be crushed they will probably be in favour of extension (of COHA).'" That's final peace, right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, intermediate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "'We offer more than the extension of the COHA; we offer final cessation of hostilities which would antecede the peace. We do not offer temporary cease-fires which have been abused (in the past) by the Muslims for re-deployment of their forces, arming themselves and other military activities which are banned during a period of cessation of hostilities. We demand permanent cessation of hostilities and renewal of the talks aimed at definite political settlement.'" [Interpretation] In your view, would you say that this statement of Dr. Karadzic speaks about war again or did he speak about peace?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic's position throughout much of the war was: First you freeze the confrontation lines, then you negotiate a settlement. Here he is re-stating that long-held position which was shared by Britain and France and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the statement given by Mr. Enrique Aguilar on the 21st of March, 1995, and then again in one given on the 25th of April, 1995, given by Dr. Karadzic, can we trace a similarity in terms that the international community did not have a solution to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's correct that the conventional view of the international community, that first there should be a cease-fire and then there should be a peace process, was a failed approach, as had been shown through the earlier plans, and a different approach would be -- should be developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the sources exactly for the statement given by Mr. Aguilar and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I mentioned it. It's document 65 ter number 10594.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, that's the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you said you would not --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the end of first paragraph and the beginning of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My problem is access to 65 ter numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you 65 ter number -- ERN number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's ZA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, even ERN numbers for the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: ERN number -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unless they are released, and we usually get access to them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to later deal with that at a certain moment because you're referring to documents to which we might not have access at this moment in the system. Please proceed meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go now to paragraph 181 of your statement. I think that once again we can agree that in spite of the Muslim offensives, the only threats that are being issued were against the Serbs and the threats constituted air-strikes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to say: "The Big Squeeze" - that's bullet point 2 in paragraph 181: "The Serbs are tightening the noose around Sarajevo. The tunnel and the road around the airport have been attacked; road access across the airport is threatened; airport negotiations are going nowhere; humanitarian aid is restricted; gas pressure has been cut; water and electricity could be next." We are speaking about the 13th of May, 1995. Can we please be shown document 3511 and it is connected with my question. Is it correct that on the day before, that is to say on the 12th of May, a major offensive was launched by the Muslim army from Sarajevo towards the Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. There was a Bosnian offensive out of Sarajevo going on about this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can't find it in the document. I can't find it in this document and I'm sure it's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is the date of the 12th, is that vital or -- because Mr. Harland said it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is vital because obviously it's just the response, not the attack by Serbs. So we want to show that all Serb actions were actually reactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please find your source.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously I cannot right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, I do understand that it's a weekly situation report --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you want what is written --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- written on the 13th to be a direct response to what happened on the 12th, then I would be a surprise because at least on this page it's a weekly report which could extend from the 6th to the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore -- again, if you want to demonstrate that it was a direct response and that the date of the 12th is vital, that seems to contradict what I see here as a weekly report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if -- please proceed [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the last day here I see 11th of May. That's why. It started with 8th and ends with 11th. Probably I will find it later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said the Muslim attack was on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document that we are looking at now, on page 2 there's this subtitle: "The Big Squeeze." You say: [In English] "The Serbs are 'squeezing' Sarajevo, perhaps in an effort to force the Bosnians to attempt a break-out from the city." [Interpretation] By saying this, did you mean that the Serbs were to blame for the Muslim offensives too? What did you mean by that sentence?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that -- there are several things. First, the Bosnian government, whether or not that was known to the Serb authorities, I don't know, had taken a decision - and we could see it unfolding - to try to break the Siege of Sarajevo during the spring of 1995. The Serbs simultaneously were applying military pressure and they were very confident of their capacity to contain it, and so I think where UNPROFOR had a concern is that all of these attacks you've listed, the shelling around the water points in Dobrinja and so on, these were the killings of civilians just going about their normal business and the cutting off of the water and electricity. But yes, it is quite possible, in our view, not certain -- we didn't claim it was certain, that the Serbs were confident enough of their capacity to resist an attack out; that they were increasing the pressure as much as possible, including by these various killings of civilians, in order to accelerate what they knew would be an unsuccessful Bosnian attempt to break the siege lines. And in a way, they were right. The Bosnians did attempt to break out and they did fail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The offensives were not launched by civilians. The offensives were launched by the Bosnian military; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the points you pointed me to, such as the mortar attack kills ten, those weren't ten soldiers. If I remember rightly, they were ten mainly elderly people trying to collect water in Dobrinja and other -- UNPROFOR never considered air-strikes for purely force-on-force military activity. It's only when the violence against civilians reached an intolerable level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that in your document of 13th of May there is no mention of civilian deaths. It only says that ten people were killed by a mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where can we find this piece of information, in which of your documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm testifying. We can probably go and get it. But I put it in. In general I didn't record military casualties at all. We got all the military casualties from the Ministry of Health and we checked them. I didn't bother putting them into a weekly situation report unless there were unusually large numbers or if they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic and Mr. Harland, on page 2, mortar attack on the tunnel, I read: "There were more than 20 casualties. Eleven people were killed. The casualties included both civilians and military personnel." Could you -- were among the people killed, which is approximately half of the casualties, were they civilians as far as you remember, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us an approximate number, was it half of the nine or the majority or a small number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular incident, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say civilians were killed, but you do not know whether it was one out of the nine or more -- well, "civilians" already is a plural --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- the exact number at this distance I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of clarity, how come that I know that the Muslim offensive started on the 12th of May? It has been mentioned in paragraph 180 of your statement you say: "I remember that on the 12th of May, 1995, or thereabouts a Bosnian offensive was launched out of Sarajevo." Therefore, I relied on your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, again I have difficulties in following you. If you say this document, on the 13th of May, clearly indicates that whatever the Serbs did was always in response to ... and you focus our attention to the 12th of May, then of course whatever appears in this document before the 12th of May could not be a response to what happened on the 12th of May. So I'm a bit confused about your line of questioning, but please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, do you want to say something, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shelling of the tunnel mentioned, it is clear namely that the Serbs knew that this tunnel was used to funnel weapons into Sarajevo. Now, do you have any information showing that the Serbs had information to the effect that the tunnel was used to funnel weapons into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically on the statement. The Serbs told us all the time that they were generally aware of what was flowing in and out of the tunnel. I believe they had sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me - or perhaps you wouldn't - that the BH Army soldiers in their presence and their weapons, their installations, offensives, jeopardised the safety of the civilian population in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to protest that sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You go on to say that in May 1995 the total zone of exclusion collapsed, the TEZ. Both sides reclaimed their weapons, correct, and began to use them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 183 of your statement toward the beginning, as it says -- as the report on Srebrenica states in paragraph 188, and this report is not in evidence, but you say: "On the 22nd of May, Bosnian Serb forces removed two heavy weapons from the weapons collection points near the city and Bosnian forces withdrew weapons of their own, the fighting escalated." As we've established, this is ten days after the major Muslim offensive was launched. We see that this was noted on the 22nd of May, whereas the offensive began on the 12th of May. Now, my question is this: Do you have any information about other Muslim units in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the units around Tuzla, Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Bihac, were also launching attacks in order to relieve the pressure on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct that there was a general effort. I don't think the purpose was to relieve pressure on Sarajevo. I think they were also trying to attack out of Sarajevo, but there was a general Bosnian offensive going on in the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this report on page 4 -- page 3, rather, my apologies, the last paragraph -- in the last paragraph you say this: [In English] "It is possible that the Serb objective is turn Sarajevo into a real enclave ..." [Interpretation] From this it is clear that up until this date Sarajevo was not an enclave per se, not in the true sense of the word; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Connected by the tunnel and the airport, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the tunnel remained under the control of the Bosnian army all through the end of the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this same paragraph, 183, you go on to say: "On the 24th of May, 1995, General Smith issued an ultimatum to the Serbs with respect to their violations in Sarajevo and threatened air-strikes -- threatened with air-strikes." Can we agree once again that on this occasion General Smith did not issue threats to the other party to the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you say that another dead-line was established before which the parties had either to remove their weapons from the total exclusion zone or place them in collection points. You say the Serbs failed to comply, ignoring the ultimatum, and in response NATO bombed certain Bosnian Serb military targets on the 25th of May. Would you agree with me that the Muslims did not comply either and did not hand over their weapons, did not deliver them to the collection points?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember at this date. That may be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move to June 1995, paragraph 195 of your statement -- 190, my apologies. We see here another offensive by the Muslim forces and you say: "On 16 June 1995 Bosnian forces began a series of attacks to break out of Sarajevo." And on this occasion, as previously, there was no request to have NATO support against these Muslim forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The threats were made against heavy weapons violations of the total exclusion zone. The normal pattern - and this was a much more serious offensive - was the Muslims had a numerical advantage and so they used their light infantry, but they were at a disadvantage on heavy weapons. When either side used heavy weapons, but the Serbs used heavy weapons more, they had more and to compensate for their lack of people, then they would be subject to threats by us and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, there was no request for NATO strikes against Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's look at paragraph 191 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, did I understand your testimony well, also at earlier stages, that at no point in time there has ever been a threat against Bosnian forces with NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Rose, who was the commander in 1994, the middle year of the war, considered it and he raised it as a possibility with Dr. Ganic and I believe with General Divjak, but he knew that it would not be approved up the hierarchy. So I think he did it more to encourage the sides. There was no serious consideration of air-strikes against the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore, certainly no threat? Threatening means you tell someone if you do this I'll --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they -- actually, they did. There were some threats made, but I don't think there was any real intention to carry through on those threats in early 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to move on to paragraph 191 of your statement. We're still in June 1995 and I would like to call document 17698. You state in this paragraph -- please bear with me. In this document, in fact, that you're -- make a reference to in your report, on page 2, the first and second paragraphs: [In English] "Heavy fighting erupts in Sarajevo on Wednesday, as both sides scramble to assert control of the BSA supply route." BSA is Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "... both sides tried to assert control over the Pale-Lukavica road." [Interpretation] That, too, is a route that was used by the Army of Republika Srpska [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnia Herzegovina"], correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the Bosniaks are attempting with this offensive to cut --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's general experience that if you read that usually the speed of speech goes up. Could you please have a look at whether everything you wanted to refer to appears on the transcript. If so, please proceed; if not, please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The transcript states that these were routes used by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's on page 28, lines 19 and 20, so I will have to repeat my question, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be a mistake there. I think you clearly -- at least it was translated to us as used by the Republika Srpska Army and that apparently was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, at the same time, I'm looking at the clock. I'd like to take a break of half an hour, but before we adjourn I have one matter to raise but we can do that in the absence of Mr. Harland. Mr. Harland, would you already follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we had some problem in - what was it? - page 7 or was it page 8, and we are talking about exhibit -- about document 8163. Now, the cause of the problem is that page 5 out of 8, both in the handwritten numbering of the pages and the numbering of the pages at the bottom of each page and the numbering of the Telefax sequence, indicate that page 5 is missing. So apparently it's an incomplete document because in all the numbering systems 5 is missing. And it could well be that it was uploaded by the Prosecution. Mr. Groome, would you please verify what caused a one missing page in every numbering system of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that when it was originally processed by the evidence unit the numbers are consecutive. So I think the thing for the Prosecution to do is go back in the vault and check the original which I will have done sometime today if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then I think page 5 didn't play a role apart from interrupting the numbering. We'll take a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We see that the witness will be escorted into the courtroom. For the next witness the Chamber has some concerns about timing and flexibility. Could you give us an indication already, Mr. Lukic, what time you think you would need for cross-examination of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next witness? My colleague is signalling me that he needs two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours. Which means that there's a reasonable expectation that we could conclude the testimony of the next witness by tomorrow and then the flexibility problem doesn't arise anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, while we're waiting for the witness to come in --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- may I just ask so that the Chamber can better understand which way we're going, I just wanted to find out -- I find your questions relate to the war rather than to war crimes with this witness, and I'm just trying to find out where we're going with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the war is part of our case as well, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's just what I want to understand. Because my understanding is I don't think that war itself is a crime or that war is charged as a crime. What is charged -- the crimes that are committed during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the -- how I've understood your questions this morning is that you're asking about what the army -- as an army does, as a Serb army or as an ABiH army, not what the individuals do by way of committing crimes or not committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we can elicit that kind of information from this witness, Your Honour, as something concrete. He was head of a civil part of UNPROFOR, so he has a knowledge about general stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct. But from what you have been reading from his statement he makes references to so many people killed, some of them civilian, some of them soldiers, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So he does make reference -- he does refer to crimes or killings that are taking place. We want to know whether -- are those charged or not charged?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We think if we show the context in which killings appeared, then it would show that it's more in fightings than as intention to kill a civilian or -- that's what we want to elicit from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to see that happening. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, we'll continue now. Apologies for dealing with other matters when you entered the courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to move on to paragraph 193 of your statement. In this paragraph you mention a document, 65 ter 17698. My apologies, 17675. In this paragraph in the document that you are referring to, in the first paragraph you say the following: [In English] "The Bosnian offensive which began last week petered out very quickly -- apparently due to heavy casualties -- but is expected to resume again in the near future." [Interpretation] In other words, UNPROFOR too was aware that the Bosniak side would relaunch and relaunch new offensives; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in the next sentence, and we've already established this, you say that the last of the UNPROFOR prisoners or hostage was released. And we've said that's what it was. Now, did UNPROFOR have information that after the release of the last hostage the air-strikes against Serb positions would resume?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Air attacks were made at UNPROFOR request; that was how the system worked. NATO didn't independently engage at all except in the air, you know, air-to-air action.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at document 11477 and this is related to paragraph 194 of your statement. When you state here that you were shown documents, orders from Karadzic dated 13th and 17th June 1995 relating to the release of hostages, it is obvious that in this procedure General Mladic's name does not appear anywhere; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on to paragraph 196 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any dispute about the name of Mr. Mladic appearing in these orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, not in document number -- or 65 ter number 11477. We agree, that's plainly visible from the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore perhaps superfluous to ask. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 196 you say the following: "The Serbs also wanted to pull out their weapons from those areas." Is it correct that the Serbs needed those weapons to defend themselves from these Bosniak offensives and not for the purpose of terrorising the civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they served both of those purposes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I propose that you quote the entire sentence and not only the part of the sentence to put it more clearly on the record and to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question covered actually the second part of the sentence because in the sentence said that the Serbs took the weaponry to continue their campaign against the civilians of Sarajevo and to force the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to make a political agreement with them. So that's -- I think that my question actually covered this part, but thank you anyways.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like you to take a look at paragraph 203 of your statement. In this paragraph you state the following: "The Bosnian offensive that started last week very soon petered out apparently due to heavy casualties but is expected to resume again in the near future." And then in this paragraph you go on to say: "The point I think I was trying to make in this document was the fact that the Bosnian offensive was principally of a military nature. It was a failure but it was directed at the Serb military." How did you draw that conclusion here in this statement, which in my view has absolutely nothing to do with what you've noted down in your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we would have observed fighting on the confrontation line. The Bosnian army would attack with light infantry. Often they would succeed initially. They would normally then be pushed back with heavy casualties by Serbs with their heavy weapons, and then the Serbs would resume this more or less indiscriminate shelling of the civilian population and there would be further restrictions on gas, water, electricity, and food, which of course was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry, but that wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you establish a nexus between the fact that the Muslim offensive was petering out and this led you to conclude that it had been directed against the military targets? I don't see any connection at all.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's a fact. We could see the Bosnian offensive taking place from our observation points, and they would direct their fire at Serb military positions. But the Serbs, in return, would direct their fire at the population -- the civilian population at large. We could see that all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see from your observation posts that Muslims were firing at civilians beyond the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- if it had happened, we would have seen it. And occasionally when there was a mortar bomb that went further, the Serbs would show it, in Grbavica, for example. But overwhelmingly Bosnian military activity was directed to the immediate Serb military front line, and the Serbs didn't even claim otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why the Serbs had requested sniper protection to be provided, in order to protect their military positions and targets?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There was certainly Bosnian sniper activity against Serb civilians, not just in Grbavica but principally there. But we're talking about these formed military offensives, which were always directed against formed military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's move quickly to July 1995, paragraph 213 of your statement, paragraph 213. In relation to this paragraph I would like to ask you the following. In July 1995, apart from a NATO air force, were the Serbian targets fired at by UNPROFOR as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] 1995.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I know there was a very major bombardment by the UNPROFOR rapid reaction force in August, but in July I can't remember. There was also in May an action by the French by land against the Serbs, but I can't remember in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in August. Now let me ask you this: Is it correct that the plans for firing at Serb positions were jointly drawn up by UNPROFOR and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was co-ordination between the initiative of Mr. Holbrooke, NATO, UNPROFOR, and the Bosnian army, that's correct, and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now paragraph 217, and we need document 100638. This is a weekly report on the situation in Sarajevo dated the 8th of July, 1995. We need page 2, and you say here in paragraph 5 towards the end --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say UNPROFOR is still unable to confirm these numbers, and you're talking about attacks on civilians, because it is unable to regain free access to city hospitals. How often was UNPROFOR denied access to the city hospitals?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 there was a problem when UNPROFOR believed that there was mortar fire coming from in and around the main Kosevo Hospital facility and we were excluded. And then there was a period in the summer of 1995 when we were not given access to the morgues to confirm casualty rates. But -- so I'm not sure of the exact number of times, but it did happen sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please now move to paragraph 220 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'd like to ask one clarifying question. If you had no access to the hospital, was that a matter of a day or days or was it for a month or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be several weeks at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Several weeks at a time. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So paragraph 220 of your statement, this weekly report -- this paragraph is predominantly pertaining to Zepa, and you say that the Bosniaks had requested for their weapons to be returned to them and that 127 pieces that had previously been surrendered to UNPROFOR were returned, but the estimate was that it was of no significant military value. Is it true that you reached this conclusion because you knew that at that point the Bosniaks in Zepa had much more and better weaponry in their possession?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you go on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please indicate the portion that he's reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate which portion you're reading; and if you read, do it a bit more slowly, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the second sentence in paragraph 220, and it starts: "During this period ..." "During the period I was heavily preoccupied with an effort to secure an international commitment to prevent the fall of Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have agreed that Zepa was not demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was meant to be demilitarised under a demilitarised agreement, but in fact it held weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you go on to say as follows, that's towards the end of the paragraph: "Resolution 836 of 4th June 1993 extended the mandate of UNPROFOR to enable it to deter attacks on the safe areas and to promote the withdrawal of military forces other than those of the Bosnian government. Neither resolution was successfully implemented." In what way were these resolutions not successfully implemented?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was in the end not possible to deter attacks on them because the Serbs never allowed sufficient troops, UNPROFOR troops, in them to make that mission credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] One second. Now what about the other party, what was it that they hadn't complied with?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we had this conversation last week. My recollection of Resolutions 817, 824, and 836 is that they do not put an obligation on the Bosnian government party to withdraw, but that in the specific case of Srebrenica and Zepa, there was a bilateral agreement between the Bosnian government and the Serbs on demilitarisation, which both sides violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to this issue. Article 3 of the agreement says that each and every military or paramilitary unit must withdraw from the demilitarised zone or surrender their weapons, the ammunition, mines, explosives, and other combat equipment. Did this surrender happen in full? Was everything surrendered to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: But as -- but, sir, you do keep saying what was an obligation -- you started to ask me what was an obligation under the Security Council Resolution, and then you quote an article from the bilateral agreement, whereas my point in the statement was that the Security Council Resolutions require one thing, which as far as I remember does not include the withdrawal or cantonment of Bosnian forces. The bilateral agreement, which I'm not even sure I mention in here, certainly did require demilitarisation and I very openly always said that both sides violated it. So if your question is not about the Security Council Resolution, it's just about the bilateral agreement Article 3, I would say, yes, it was violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since this agreement was signed on the 8th of May, 1993, in the presence of General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have document 5681, and it is related to paragraph 222 of your statement. You say that civilian leaders in enclave began to negotiate surrender terms with the Serbs; however, government authorities in Sarajevo insisted that the negotiation -- negotiators were not authorised. Is it true that the Sarajevo authorities by means of this move wished for the fighting in Zepa to continue?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that the Bosnian government representatives, both President Izetbegovic and Dr. Muratovic, told me that they did not accept that the civilian authorities of Zepa had the authority to surrender the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now paragraph 223 of your statement -- actually, this paragraph is related to the document that we have on our screens. Last paragraph on page 1 reads: [In English] "Bosnian government forces have stated that UNPROFOR troops in Zepa will 'share the fate' of the enclave, implying that they will use the UNPROFOR troops as human shields in the event of a Serb assault. They have overrun and disarmed a number of UNPROFOR observation posts." [Interpretation] We know from before that no request for assistance was made to NATO with respect to this kind of actions of the Bosniak army. But I'd like to ask you this: What happened to the people at those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a small Ukrainian unit I think in Zepa. They radioed us to say that the Bosniaks were afraid that if the Serbs overran it they would be massacred and they were holding them as a sort of human shield against it. In the end what happened was the -- I believe the civilian -- an agreement was managed so the civilian population largely left unharmed. When the Bosniaks didn't agree to the military surrender, General Mladic killed Avdo Palic or ordered his killing, and then -- or at least they told us they had killed him. And then when they saw there was no option, in fact the Bosnians escaped over the river to Serbia, I believe, and they left the Ukrainian UNPROFOR troops unharmed, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then on the next page of this document you say the following -- we'll go back to paragraph 1 on page 2. Let's go back for a second to Avdo Palic. You said that General Mladic killed him or maybe ordered his murder?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who provided you with this information?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, General Tolimir. We were asked whether we could bring Palic to the Serb observation point for discussion under a flag of truce. Palic agreed. He wanted to do that to help the civilians survive. And then, in our presence, when Palic refused to surrender the military component, they took him away. And when we asked to see him, General Tolimir said, "He's dead." So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long was it between the time when you saw him and the time when Tolimir told you that he was dead?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know that after that he was transferred to Bijeljina to the Batkovic military camp?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that -- what they told us, which is that he's dead, and I understand that he is dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to raise this issue with someone who has more information. Thank you anyway. First paragraph on the next page you say the following: [In English] "We recommend that UNPROFOR propose an immediate and complete demilitarisation of the Zepa safe area, to be implemented under UNPROFOR supervision within 48 hours of agreement ..." [Interpretation] Let me first ask you this: You believed that demilitarisation of Zepa was possible to be completed within 48 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a small place, not many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the truth is that demilitarisation had not been completed for more than two years, despite the agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1993 demilitarisation agreement had not been implemented, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You knew that this part of the agreement wasn't fulfilled because the Serbs complained to UNPROFOR about this not having been done?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And until this date, neither UNPROFOR nor you personally did anything with regard to this issue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. So both sides were in constant standing violation of the 1993 demilitarisation agreement. We constantly raised it with both parties and both parties continued to be in violation. That was one of the reasons that we, in the end, moved to a more direct use of force policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and this document exactly shows what proposals are concerned here. You say that if the Bosnian government accepts the agreement and the Bosnian Serbs refuse, Pale will be informed about the decision of 22nd April 1994, that their military positions and backup positions, including fuel depots and ammunition depots, would be subject to NATO strikes. So that was your proposal, unless the Serbs comply with and the Bosniaks do comply with, we are going to bomb the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you say the following: "Should the Bosnian government refuse to comply ..." Basically what you are saying that you wouldn't be very happy with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this occasion, again you do not issue any threats to the Bosnian side, any threats of NATO air-strikes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct because we wanted the force to be principally used against the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, is this position an objective one and is that position that you subscribe to?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was factually, morally, and legally very complicated, but for me the heart of the UNPROFOR mandate was to deter attacks on six safe areas by all means necessary. We had discovered over a period of over two years that it was impossible to deter those attacks by any other means than force, but that the Serbs responded only and relatively well to the use of force or at least to the credible threat of the use of force. So yes, I believe it was objectively in line with my duty to try to advise on the implementation of the UNPROFOR mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this position of yours, objective, as you say, is visible in all of your reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think, like others, I started from the view that we should first negotiate a cease-fire; and then that would create space for the great powers to mediate a final peace settlement. It was only in 1995 that a group, including myself, came to the conclusion that it would not be possible to fulfil the mandate unless a more robust use of the UNPROFOR mandate were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Against one side alone, the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think your point is clear, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we have paragraph 225, please. And this is related to document 65 ter 09322. And here you only talk about the second document or just the first, rather, but I will put some questions to you about the second document. Can we have this document on the screen, please, that's 09322. This is another document that was sent by you. And we need to see the second page. And here again we find in the sixth paragraph from the top or the second from the bottom where you say: "At about the same time the Ukrainians in Zepa reported that Bosnian forces had begun to attack their compound with small arms, heavy machine-guns, and rocket-propelled grenades. I called the office of Prime Minister Silajdzic immediately thereafter and warned him that such an attack or similar attacks could only harm the interests of Bosnians, especially in light of tomorrow's meeting in London." We see that here you are also concerned about the international interests of the Bosnian government in Sarajevo. Did you at any point issue warnings of this type to the Serb side and could you show us the document, if so? Well, you don't have to show it. You can just tell us.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my warning to Dr. Silajdzic was that if they kept shooting at -- the Bosnian army kept shooting at UNPROFOR positions, it would be much harder for us to argue in the London meeting for much more broad authority to use force against the Serbs. So our argument was that it was in his interest because we were hoping to get a much accelerated, much expanded, authorisation to use force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also in his interest?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move briefly to August 1995, that's paragraph 229. You are talking here about the 28th of August, 1995, and the incident at the Markale market. First I would like to remind you - and perhaps you will agree with me - that you, in fact, confuse Markale I and Markale II because Markale II that you're talking about here, there were no stalls at the market. The shell exploded outside the market grounds. Would you agree that you actually conflated these two events?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were -- there were definitely -- there were definitely casualties around the -- in the market area where had stalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you say so. We will deal with Markale I and II or perhaps just one because there's only one Markale incident mentioned in the indictment. However, I would now like to show you document 3830. The document is dated 29th August 1995. It's an UNPROFOR document. And under paragraph 3 it says: "None of the UN observers [as interpreted] in the general area along this portion of the separation line observed or heard any firing at the time of the incident ..." Would it be possible -- is it possible that not a single person from the observation post would hear or see the fire -- the shots being fired from Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would certainly be aware of the firing if it was close to the confrontation line. If it was from deeper inside Serb territory, not necessarily. This is not a document written by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to avoid confusion in the future, I do note that the document -- the subject line is the 28th of August and I believe Mr. Lukic has said the 29th of August so I don't -- the transcript records him as having said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is dated the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The 29th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, very small, at least in the English version at the top, it says date: 29th, and then subject 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I see that now, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will put it to you now that such a claim is actually running counter to the report prepared by the French observers, that's document 65 ter 10243.
